articles.title: BBRES RNG: A Scheduler Driven Approach to Random Bit Generation
articles.abstract:
BBRES-RNG began with a systems question: can the order in which many threads reach a shared synchronization point be turned into a useful bit-generation process? I built the project in Java as a layered design: worker threads contend for a synchronized allocator, the observed assignment order is reduced to bits, and rejection sampling maps those bits into a requested integer range. The result is a distinctive exploration of concurrency as a source of runtime variation, combining thread scheduling, identifier ordering, XOR reduction, and bounded sampling in one pipeline.

Project focus: BBRES-RNG is an engineering experiment in converting execution order into data. Its distinctive contribution is the way it connects a hierarchical thread race to a bit-selection and integer-generation pipeline.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.body: This article analyzes the supplied BBRES-RNG v1.2.0 Java source, two architecture diagrams, and the BBRES-RNG Combined Validation Report dated July 25, 2026. It reconstructs the bit-generation path from worker creation through scheduler-sensitive assignment, XOR reduction, and bounded-range sampling. It then summarizes the report's bit-level, integer-level, prediction, and entropy analyses, including the Cramér–von Mises failure and the report's own SP 800-90B caveats. The central engineering question is not whether the output looks random in a finite battery, but whether the scheduling process can be modeled, measured, and shown to supply sufficient entropy across platforms and restarts.

sections.heading: The Design Question
sections.body:
Random number generation is usually presented as either a deterministic algorithm with an internal state or a physical measurement whose output varies with a noise source. BBRES-RNG explores a different systems surface: the runtime order of competing threads. A Java process creates groups of workers, releases them to contend for a synchronised operation, and records which worker identifier reaches the allocator first, next, and last.

This approach turns familiar building blocks: threads, locks, arrays, XOR, and range sampling into an unusual composition. The project is not simply a wrapper around a standard generator. It makes scheduling order part of the bit-generation path and provides two modes that vary how worker identifiers are presented to that race.

sections.heading: Architecture at a Glance
sections.body: The implementation separates the process into levels. The outer initializer prepares identifiers and divides them into groups. Each group starts worker threads and releases them to compete. The group reduces selected identifiers to an intermediate value; the outer level combines group values into one output bit. The integer API repeats the bit-generation operation to form a candidate and accepts only candidates inside the requested range. (Refer to the architecture diagrams attached below.)

sections.heading: How a Bit is Generated?
sections.body:
• Prepare and partition worker identifiers:
    • In the supplied v1.2.0 source, the public RNG methods default to a worker parameter n of 71. The accepted configured range is 3 through 1000; invalid values fall back to the default. The initializer chooses a number of groups around a target chunk size of 32 and caps the number of groups at 32. Each group receives a slice of the identifier array.

      Mode 1 uses identifiers in their initialized order. Mode 2 first shuffles them with a Fisher–Yates pass driven by a helper BBRES-RNG implementation, then distributes the shuffled identifiers to groups. This gives the design two ways to shape the relationship between worker identity and the order in which workers reach the allocator.
  • Release workers into the allocator:
    • Each group initializer creates one worker thread per identifier in its slice. Workers wait on a group-specific flag using a spin-wait loop. Once released, every worker calls the shared synchronized allocator. That method scans the group's section of a shared array and places the worker's identifier into the first available slot.

      The synchronized method serializes writes, while the order in which contending workers enter the critical section determines the sequence of identifiers recorded in those slots. In this way, the implementation captures a race in lock acquisition order without allowing simultaneous writes to corrupt the shared array.
  • Reduce an assignment order to a bit:
    • When the workers in a group have finished, the group initializer computes a cut size equal to 20 percent of the group, rounded up. It XORs the identifiers in the first and last cut-sized regions of the assignment array, then applies a short series of XOR and shift operations. The resulting group values are XORed together by the outer initializer, and the least significant bit becomes the generated output bit.

      Selecting both ends of the assignment order makes the group result depend on worker identifiers that arrived near the beginning and end of the race. Mode 2 changes the identifier-to-worker mapping before the race; the reduction stage then processes the resulting order in the same way.

sections.heading: From Generated Bits to Bounded Integers
sections.body:
The public API supports a default range, an upper bound, or explicit minimum and maximum values. For a requested interval, the implementation computes the span, generates a candidate bit string long enough to represent that span, converts the string to an integer, masks off the sign bit, and rejects values above the span. An accepted candidate is offset by the requested minimum.

This is rejection sampling. If candidate bit strings are uniformly distributed, accepting only values within the requested span avoids the modulo bias that can occur when a random integer is reduced with a remainder operation. The validation report tests integer output over the inclusive range [0, 1000].

sections.heading: What makes BBRES-RNG Distinctive?
sections.body:
The project's defining idea is that runtime coordination itself can be made part of the generator's data path. Instead of reading a timer directly, BBRES-RNG creates controlled contention and records the order in which threads pass through a synchronized allocator. The implementation then transforms that ordering into a bit through group selection, XOR reduction, and bit extraction.

Three design choices give the project its character:

  • First, the hierarchy scales the experiment from many workers to one bit.
  • Second, two identifier modes let the system compare direct ordering with a shuffled input order.
  • Third, rejection sampling connects the bit stream to a practical integer API without relying on modulo reduction.

That combination makes BBRES-RNG useful as a systems research project even apart from its statistical outcome. It invites investigation of how JVM scheduling, lock contention, group size, worker count, and machine load affect the observed ordering. It also creates concrete questions about how such a software-visible process should be measured and modeled as an entropy source.

sections.heading: Engineering Considerations
sections.body:
The design intentionally creates many short-lived threads, so thread creation and coordination are central costs. A natural engineering study is to compare the current thread-per-worker structure with reusable executors or barriers, while measuring whether a change preserves the ordering signal that the generator is designed to observe. The synchronized allocator is another key point: it protects shared state and makes acquisition order observable, while also becoming a serialization point.

The implementation keeps configuration and coordination arrays in shared static state. This makes the prototype straightforward to explore through simple public methods, while also making invocation lifecycle and concurrent callers important areas for future design work. These trade-offs are useful engineering questions because they connect the RNG's central idea directly to real Java concurrency behaviour.

Observed throughput: In one console run, BBRES-RNG generated 20 million bits in 225,286.89 seconds (approximately 88.8 bits per second). A separate 100,000-bit run measured about 37.3 bits per second. These are individual observations; throughput may vary with run conditions.

sections.heading: Validation Results
sections.body: A sample of 31,377,615 generated bits and 500,000 integers in [0, 1000]. Across its 54 reported checks, 53 passed. This includes core and extended bitstream tests, distribution and spectral checks, prediction experiments, integer-distribution and sequence checks, and a non-IID min-entropy analysis. (Detailed report attached below.)
